question:
Patient note:
A 91-year-old woman who lives with a hired daytime aide in a single-story cottage was brought directly to the surgical intensive care holding bay by paramedics after the aide noticed progressive abdominal distention and two episodes of nonbloody, nonbilious emesis early this morning; according to the electronic record she carries long-standing hypertension, osteoarthritis of the knees, and stage 3 chronic kidney disease with outpatient serum creatinine values fluctuating between 1.6 and 1.8 mg/dL over the past three years, but she has never required dialysis and has no history of organ transplantation, cytotoxic chemotherapy, prolonged corticosteroid exposure, or advanced cardiac, pulmonary, or hepatic failure. Her medication list includes amlodipine, low-dose aspirin, and acetaminophen as needed for joint pain; she takes no diuretics, inhalers, or immunomodulators. The aide reports that the patient ate normally until two days ago, when she became nauseated and reduced her oral intake to sips of water; last night she complained of crampy periumbilical discomfort and had one small watery stool, then awoke at dawn with worsening bloating and confusion about the day of the week, prompting the emergency call. Emergency medical services arrived nine minutes after activation: they found her sitting forward in a dining-room chair, pale but speaking in full sentences, with fingertip oxygen saturation of 86 % on room air. The crew applied a fixed-performance Venturi collar delivering 44 % inspired oxygen, placed an 18-gauge peripheral catheter without initiating fluids, and administered no analgesics, antiemetics, antibiotics, or vasoactive agents during the twelve-minute suburban transport. Upon stretcher entry to the unit—and before any hospital intervention—the initial set of vitals showed an oral temperature of 37.1 °C, a regular heart rate of 81 beats per minute on three-lead telemetry, respirations visually counted at 12 breaths per minute without accessory-muscle use, and a non-invasive blood pressure cycling at 134/72 mm Hg on repeat cuff confirmation. Skin examination revealed mild tenting over the clavicles and dry mucous membranes but no mottling or peripheral cyanosis; capillary refill was just over two seconds. Jugular venous pulsations were not elevated at 30°, and distal pulses were 2+ bilaterally. Cardiac auscultation disclosed a crisp S1, single S2, and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. The abdomen was markedly distended, tympanitic, and moderately tender in the midline without rebound or guarding; high-pitched tinkling bowel sounds were audible, and an irreducible 3-cm right femoral bulge was noted beneath thin skin, suggesting a possible obstructed hernia. There was no surgical scar, no flank ecchymosis, and no costovertebral angle tenderness. Extremities were without edema, clubbing, or petechiae. Neurologically, she opened her eyes to her name, uttered confused phrases though able to state her own first name, and obeyed simple one-step commands, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 13 in the absence of sedatives, alcohol, or head trauma. Six minutes after arrival, a right radial arterial specimen drawn while she remained on the same 44 % mask yielded a pH of 7.30, PaCO₂ 37 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 55 mm Hg; end-tidal capnography displayed 36 mm Hg, indicating appropriate ventilatory matching. Simultaneous point-of-care chemistry recorded sodium 159 mmol/L, potassium 4.55 mmol/L, chloride 114 mmol/L, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, glucose 112 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 34 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.75 mg/dL, essentially equivalent to her documented baseline and therefore not representing an acute rise. A complete blood count returned white blood cells 11 900 /mm³ with 78 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 42 %, hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL, and platelets 248 000 /µL. Venous lactate performed at bedside measured 2.0 mmol/L. A portable supine abdominal radiograph obtained before any nasogastric decompression demonstrated multiple dilated small-bowel loops with air-fluid levels and minimal colonic gas; chest imaging done concurrently showed clear lung fields apart from bibasilar atelectasis and a normal cardiac silhouette. Bedside focused cardiac ultrasound revealed a small but vigorously contracting left ventricle with an inferior vena cava diameter of 1.1 cm collapsing more than 50 % with quiet inspiration, supporting intravascular depletion rather than overload. Bladder scan indicated 60 mL, and she had not voided since early the previous evening. Electrocardiography printed during the arterial draw showed normal sinus rhythm at 82 beats per minute, PR interval 160 ms, QRS 92 ms, and flattened lateral T waves without acute ischemia. Importantly, at the moment the critical-care team assumed responsibility—approximately twenty-five minutes after stretcher roll-in—she had received no intravenous crystalloid, no opioids, no antiemetics, no anticoagulants, no antibiotics, no vasopressors, and no endoscopic or surgical intervention; the only ongoing therapy remained the Venturi device set at 44 % oxygen. Thus, the physiologic and laboratory data at untreated presentation stand as follows: temperature 37.1 °C, systolic pressure 134 mm Hg, diastolic pressure 72 mm Hg, heart rate 81 beats/min, respiratory rate 12 breaths/min, arterial pH 7.30, serum sodium 159 mmol/L, serum potassium 4.55 mmol/L, creatinine 1.75 mg/dL, hematocrit 42 %, white blood cell count 11 900 /mm³, inspired oxygen fraction 44 %, and arterial oxygen tension 55 mm Hg—findings consistent with obstructive small-bowel pathology complicated by dehydration, mild systemic inflammation, hypernatremia, stable chronic kidney dysfunction, and hypoxemic respiratory insufficiency likely related to atelectasis in the setting of abdominal distention rather than intrinsic pulmonary disease.

Question: What is the patient's APACHE II score?
solution:
APACHE II adds acute physiology, age, and chronic health points. Using the available presentation measurements:
- Temperature 37.1 °C: 0; mean arterial pressure (134 + 2 × 72)/3 ≈ 93 mm Hg: 0; heart rate 81/min: 0; respiratory rate 12/min: 0.
- FiO₂ 0.44 is below 0.50, so use PaO₂ rather than the alveolar–arterial gradient. PaO₂ 55 mm Hg (55–60): 3.
- Arterial pH 7.30 (7.25–7.32): 2. Do not also score bicarbonate.
- Sodium 159 mmol/L (155–159): 2; potassium 4.55 mmol/L: 0.
- Creatinine 1.75 mg/dL (1.5–1.9): 2. It is at baseline, so no doubling for acute renal failure.
- Hematocrit 42%: 0; WBC 11,900/mm³: 0; neurologic points = 15 − GCS 13 = 2.
Acute physiology subtotal = 3 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 11. Age 91 (≥75) adds 6. There is no qualifying severe chronic organ failure or immunosuppression, so chronic health adds 0. Total = 11 + 6 + 0 = 17.
Final answer: 17
